Case 3: cadmium in the soil
In the late 1940s a disease characterized by extreme
generalized pain, kidney damage, and loss of bone
strength appeared in the Jinzu River Basin. The dis-
ease, which primarily afflicted women, was called itai-
itai (''It hurts, it hurts!'') after the cries of the sufferers.
Two decades of research led, in 1968, to the conclusion
that the cause was chronic cadmium poisoning, which
was traced to the effluent from the Mitsui Mining and
Smelting Company located in the upper reaches of the
basin. The route for the cadmium poisoning was from
river water to irrigation water to soil to rice. By 1991,
129 people had been certified as itai-itai sufferers, and
116 of them had died.
A major program of soil restoration was initiated in
1979. By 1992, 36 percent of the contaminated area of
1,500 hectares had been treated. Had the further re-
lease of cadmium not been prevented, the annual costs
from medical compensation, agricultural losses, and
soil restoration would have been $19 million a year. The
costs of prevention were $5 million a year.
